claims.text: The initial (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy contains microcracks and moderate porosity.
The initial alloy has a significant magnetocaloric effect.
HIP at approximately 900–1000 °C and 150–200 MPa for 1–2 hours is a suitable densification schedule for this alloy.
A 5–10 minute anneal at 700–800 °C will relieve residual stress in the HIP-treated alloy.
A brief anneal at 700–800 °C will produce partial recrystallization.
The proposed HIP and annealing schedule will avoid major phase transformations.
HIP will eliminate or substantially reduce internal porosity.
HIP will reduce microcracks in the alloy.
The treatment will form stable, partially recrystallized grain boundaries.
The partially recrystallized grain-boundary structure will inhibit crack propagation.
Reducing pores and microcracks will remove sites for crack initiation.
Partial recrystallization will increase local ductility.
The treatment will preserve the magnetic exchange interactions responsible for the caloric response.
The treatment will not materially shift the magnetostructural transition temperature.
The treatment will increase compressive strength by at least 50% relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will improve fracture resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
The magnetocaloric adiabatic-temperature or isothermal-entropy change will decrease by no more than approximately 10%.
The processed alloy will retain a transition temperature below approximately 400 K.
The unprocessed alloy has compressive strengths of 50–220 MPa depending on epoxy or indium compositing.
Secondary phases formed during HIP or annealing could degrade caloric performance or cause embrittlement.

contradictions.description: The baseline is called the unprocessed or unchanged alloy, but its stated 50–220 MPa strength range is attributed to epoxy- and indium-composited materials, which are modified materials rather than the untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 control.
